items.title: Headlines for November 16, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## U.S. Air Travelers Continue to Face Canceled or Delayed Flights After Nationwide Ground Stop Order Nov 16, 2026 U.S. air travelers continue to face canceled or delayed flights today after a weekend of travel chaos sparked by a nationwide ground-stop order that halted domestic flights for about four hours on Friday. It was the biggest disruption to U.S. air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks. More than 12,000 flights were canceled throughout the weekend; thousands more faced delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize for the cancellations during several public appearances. Duffy blamed a contractor doing maintenance to upgrade old copper wire to fiber-optic cable, and also blamed the travel chaos on prior presidential administrations and called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to modernize air traffic control systems. Democrats pointed to $12.5 billion already approved by the Republican-controlled Congress for Department of Transportation upgrades and said the Trump administration had only spent about $1 billion of those funds. Meanwhile, two people were injured on Saturday night when two planes collided on the tarmac while taxiing at Miami International Airport. ## Iran Launches Attack on Bahrain, Targeting Radar Positions Nov 16, 2026 Iran launched an attack on Bahrain early Sunday, the latest strike on the kingdom, as clashes between Iran and the U.S. continue while peace talks remain stalled. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted radar positions at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base with six drones. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Bahrain is officially home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, though the Pentagon largely abandoned its base there after it was heavily damaged by Iranian attacks in the opening days of the U.S. war on Iran. ... forces have quietly hit several Iranian targets, among them Qeshm Island, which houses a major Revolutionary Guard naval facility. ... ## Yemeni Government Forces Retreat to Defend Aden from Houthis ... In Yemen, forces aligned with the internationally recognized government announced Sunday they were retreating from areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait in order to focus on defending their interim capital, Aden. It’s a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis. The retreat came as Houthi forces pushed to within 40 miles of Aden. Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday the Houthis had unilaterally released hundreds of prisoners. ... The remains of an estimated 8,000 Palestinians are believed to still be trapped in the rubble after more ... ## Death Toll from U.S. Measles Outbreak Rises to 10 Nov 16, 2026 The death toll from the measles outbreak in the U.S. has jumped to at least 10, as more infections erupt across several states. Wisconsin health officials reported the death of a child Friday, marking the second measles-related death in the state so far this year. On the same day, officials in Pennsylvania said an unvaccinated resident had died of measles. This comes as the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization revoked the designation amid an unprecedented measles outbreak nationwide with more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases this year. The rapid spread of measles cases comes as Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has backed anti-vaccine policies.

items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 16, 2026
items.excerpt: 16 November 2026• Update: 16 November 2026 Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including a joint call by Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK on Israel to allow urgent humanitarian aid into Gaza, the reported deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and the interception of drones over Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions with Yemen's Houthis. The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom urged Israel to "stop the delays now" and permit the immediate entry of 150,000 tents and critical supplies into Gaza ahead of winter. "We ... are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire," the top diplomats said in a joint statement. Noting that recent flooding from the first winter storm has compounded civilian suffering, the ministers warned that border restrictions are blocking desperately needed shelter and relief materials. They stressed that the crisis remains "entirely reversible" before harsher weather sets in, calling on Israel to open border crossings and grant entry to "dual-use items" required for humanitarian operations and early recovery "before it is too late." The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt will join two other US aircraft carriers in the Middle East within the next day, bringing the total American carrier presence in the region to three, the New York Times reported, citing a US military official. The deployment comes as Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in three days, ending a roughly two-month lull in hostilities while peace negotiations with Washington remain stalled. The strike followed an incident on Friday in which US forces intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward the Gulf nation. Neither the Pentagon nor the US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has issued an official confirmation regarding the carrier's deployment schedule. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi group over the Mecca region and two drones over the Medina region in western Saudi Arabia, bringing the number of drones intercepted during the day to seven. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki announced the interceptions in separate statements on the US social media platform X. He did not identify who launched the drones intercepted over Medina or provide details on possible injuries or damage. On X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree rejected the coalition’s account of the interceptions, calling it “a lie and a fabrication.”

items.title: Economic Week Ahead: Inflation, Fed Minutes and Nvidia Earnings Take Centre Stage | Investing.com
items.excerpt: Published 11/16/2026, 02:11 AM Last week’s inflation data ran hot. October’s headline CPI rose 0.4% m/m, while the core CPI rose 0.3% for a third straight month. The PPI for final demand rose 0.3% m/m in October after a revised 1.4% in September, lifting the y/y rate to 6.5%, the highest since November 2022. This week’s calendar is busy, with the FOMC minutes, Nvidia’s (NASDAQ: NVDA) earnings, Anthropic’s IPO, retail sales, and industrial production. Here’s more: ## 1. FOMC minutes & FedSpeak Minutes of the October 27-28 FOMC meeting (Wed) should show how many of the 19 participants (12 voters and 7 nonvoters) leaned toward a rate hike. The Committee held the federal funds rate (FFR) target range at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 vote, with Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a 25bps increase. Six Fed officials speak this week (Warsh, Williams, Musalem, Hammack, Goolsbee, and Paulson). Fed Chair Kevin Warsh appears Monday at the Fed’s AI and productivity task force hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area. New York Fed President John Williams, who speaks Monday and Wednesday, said on Thursday that “inflation is far too high” and that further tightening will be needed. We think the Fed should and will hike by 50bps in December. FFR futures imply 3.6 rate hikes of 25 bps over the next 12 months, including 2.6 over the next six months (chart). The odds of a 50bps hike at the December meeting are just 11.5% currently. The 2-year Treasury bond yield is at 4.86%, well above the 4.00% top of the FFR target range, with 12-month futures at 4.78% (chart).

items.title: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid warns inflation remains too hot
items.excerpt: Jeffrey Schmid, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, said Sunday central bank officials have “work to do” to rein in persistent inflation. “As Chairman Kevin Warsh said at the Kansas City Fed’s Jackson Hole Economic Symposium in August, the Fed has some work to do on inflation, and, unfortunately, our work has only gotten harder since then,” Schmid said at a National Credit Union Management Association conference in Hawaii. “Inflation has been running too hot,” he added. Schmid said that annual inflation, which rose to 3.6 percent in September according to the personal consumption expenditures price index, was “uncomfortably above” the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. Another inflation metric, the consumer price index (CPI), measured prices as up 3.7 percent year over year in September. The CPI increased by 0.4 percent from September to October, but the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to collect enough data in October 2025 — as a result of the record-long government shutdown that took up the entirety of that month — to provide annual inflation data. Schmid cited four reasons for persistently elevated inflation: energy price shocks amid the Iran war, increases in durable goods prices, the artificial intelligence build-out and mounting healthcare costs for employers and ObamaCare enrollees. The Kansas City Fed president said the central bank has the tools to address these price pressures, noting inflation “is always the result of an imbalance” between supply and demand. “It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation,” Schmid added. Schmid does not sit on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which will meet Dec. 8-9. The panel hiked interest rates by a quarter point in September, as officials seek to bring inflation down to 2 percent. At last month’s FOMC meeting, officials held rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. Traders are pricing in a 92.4 percent chance of officials raising rates in early December by a quarter point, and a 7.6 percent chance of a half-point hike, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

items.title: Treasury yields fall as investors await comments from Fed Chair Warsh
items.excerpt: Treasury yields inched lower on Monday after facing upward pressure last week, as investors awaited comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh later in the session. The 10-year Treasury yield Add To Watchlist — the key benchmark for mortgages, loans and credit card debt — was down more than 2 basis points at 5.131%, having reached a high of 5.174% on Friday before easing to 5.143%. The 2-year Treasury note yield Add To Watchlist, usually more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was more than 2 basis points lower at 4.848%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield Add To Watchlist was at 5.462%, down by more than 1 basis point. One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Warsh is set to speak later on Monday on the impact of technology on productivity and jobs. His comments will come after data last week showed the producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices, was up by less than expected in October. But the index is at its highest level in nearly four years, and expectations that cost pressure could be passed on to consumers, and further fuel inflation, intensified pressure on Treasurys last week. Retail sales, housing starts and jobless claims will be in focus this week, as inflation remains a concern. Traders expect new retail sales figures to show growth of 0.6% for October, slightly lower than September's 0.8% rise. September's data was in large part due to a 6.4% increase in gasoline sales off the back of higher prices. The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October meeting, where it left rates unchanged, will be released Wednesday. Markets have largely priced in a quarter percentage point hike in December, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

items.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
items.excerpt: Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy. Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target. He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips. By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential. Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

items.excerpt: Oil prices dropped on Monday as signs of recovering oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reinforced ​expectations of surplus supply, though ​fresh tanker incidents underscored risks ​to Middle East exports. Brent futures Add To Watchlist fell 69 cents, or 0.7%, to $95.15 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Add To Watchlist crude dropped 37 cents, or 0.4%, to $88.19. The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter ⁠of ‌this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle ⁠East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. "For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness," said KCM Trade's Waterer. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per ‌day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes ​from a record release of oil from its members' emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million ... items.excerpt: ## DOJ warns senator Warren about potential Trump-related probes Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, was warned by the US Department of ⁠Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into ​president Donald Trump. items.title: Culture: Your Monday Catch-up | AnewZ
items.excerpt: From Rosalía’s historic Latin Grammy win to Azerbaijan’s film festival success and Johnny Depp’s box office comeback, here’s your AnewZ Daily Brief for 16 November 2026, covering the biggest cultural stories from the weekend. ##### Rosalía makes Latin Grammy history with third Album of the Year win Rosalía stole the show at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, winning five awards, including her third Album of the Year title. The Spanish superstar also claimed Song of the Year and Best Pop Song for “ La Perla”, alongside Best Alternative Music Album and Best Short Form Music Video for “ Sauvignon Blanc”, making her the night's biggest winner. ##### Azerbaijani film wins top prize at international festival in The Hague Azerbaijani short film “ The Dance of Triumph” has claimed the top prize in the Global Peace, Harmony and Human Rights category at the 2026 International Film Festival The Hague. Written and directed by Garay Hasan, the film tells the story of a war veteran who lost both legs and is struggling to rebuild his life while keeping a promise to a fallen friend. A 13-member jury unanimously chose the film as the winner, praising its compelling storyline, strong performances and outstanding aesthetics. The festival attracted 503 submissions, with 63 films from 23 countries chosen for the final programme. ##### Philippines makes history with first Eurovision Asia victory The Philippines has made history after winning the first-ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia, held in Bangkok, Thailand, where 11 countries competed for the title. Singer Carmelle, 19, secured the historic victory with her women’s empowerment anthem “ Sobra-Sobra”, scoring 211 points – 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote. Thailand’s MANG x DAOU took second place with 170 points. ##### Johnny Depp tops box office for first time in eight years with 'Ebenezer' Johnny Depp has returned to the top of the North American box office for the first time in eight years, with his latest film, “ Ebenezer”, debuting at No. 1. The Charles Dickens-inspired production brought in an estimated $19 million in North America and $23 million internationally, taking its worldwide opening earnings to $42 million. Directed by Ti West, the film drew mixed reviews, scoring 52 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences, however, responded more positively, with 65 per cent of ticket buyers saying they would definitely recommend it to friends. ##### Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman honoured with Oscars Hollywood icons Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman were presented with honorary Oscars at the 17th Governors Awards in Los Angeles on Sunday, celebrating their outstanding contributions to cinema. The ceremony also marked a historic first, as Killer Films co-founders Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler became the first all-female producing team to receive the Irving G.
